lines.text: You can know useful facts about two roots without calculating either root.

For a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero, with a is not equal to zero and roots alpha, beta, factor as a open bracket x minus alpha close bracket open bracket x minus beta close bracket. Comparing coefficients gives alpha plus beta equals minus b over a and alpha beta equals c over a. These are the sum and product of roots. The negative sign belongs only in the sum.
This uses factorisation from ordinary quadratics and supplies S and P for every later calculation.
S equals alpha plus beta equals minus b over a for a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero. P equals alpha beta equals c over a and a is not equal to zero.
Why does the formula for the sum have a minus sign but the product does not?
Expressions in both roots can be found from just their sum and product.

Set S equals alpha plus beta and P equals alpha beta. Expand S squared to obtain alpha squared plus beta squared equals S squared minus two P. Expand S cubed and collect cross terms to obtain alpha cubed plus beta cubed equals S cubed minus three P S. Substitute S equals minus b over a and P equals c over a only after choosing the identity. If P is not equal to zero, reciprocals obey one over alpha plus one over beta equals S over P.
These symmetric identities provide the sums needed when forming equations with squared, cubed or reciprocal roots.
alpha squared plus beta squared equals S squared minus two P. alpha cubed plus beta cubed equals S cubed minus three P S. If P is not equal to zero, one over alpha plus one over beta equals S over P.
Where does the three P S term in the sum of cubes identity come from?
A new quadratic is determined by the sum and product of its new roots.

If the transformed roots are u, v, find T equals u plus v and U equals u v, then form x squared minus T x plus U equals zero. Clear denominators across the whole equation. For u equals alpha cubed, v equals beta cubed, T equals S cubed minus three P S and U equals P cubed. For reciprocal roots, T equals S over P and U equals one over P, requiring P is not equal to zero. For u equals alpha plus two over alpha, v equals beta plus two over beta, first expand both the sum and product, then replace alpha over beta plus beta over alpha by open bracket S squared minus two P close bracket over P.
The coefficient identities give S, P, symmetric manipulation gives T, U, together they produce the new equation.

Find transformed sum T and product U. Form x squared minus T x plus U equals zero and clear denominators. Reciprocal transformations require P is not equal to zero. For one over alpha squared, one over beta squared, require P is not equal to zero, T equals open bracket alpha squared plus beta squared close bracket over open bracket alpha squared beta squared close bracket equals open bracket S squared minus two P close bracket over P squared and U equals one over P squared. For alpha plus two over beta, beta plus two over alpha, require P is not equal to zero, T equals S plus two S over P and U equals P plus two plus two plus four over P equals P plus four plus four over P.

two Roots of quadratic equations.
In one breath.

A quadratic's coefficients tell you the sum and product of its roots without solving it. Those two quantities are enough to evaluate many symmetric expressions and to form equations whose roots are transformed versions of the originals.
Key ideas.

Suppose a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero, where a is not equal to zero, has roots alpha and beta. Factorisation gives a open bracket x minus alpha close bracket open bracket x minus beta close bracket equals a x squared minus a open bracket alpha plus beta close bracket x plus a alpha beta. Comparing coefficients, write. S equals alpha plus beta equals minus b over a, P equals alpha beta equals c over a. These identities hold whether the roots are distinct, repeated, real or complex. The minus sign in the sum is essential. If the equation is not monic, divide by a or keep the divisions explicitly. For example, two x squared minus seven x plus three equals zero has S equals seven over two and P equals three over two, you need not find either root.

A symmetric root expression is unchanged when alpha and beta are exchanged. Rewrite it in S and P before substituting numbers. From S squared equals alpha squared plus two alpha beta plus beta squared, alpha squared plus beta squared equals S squared minus two P. Expanding S cubed and collecting the cross terms gives. alpha cubed plus beta cubed equals S cubed minus three P S. Similarly, provided P is not equal to zero, one over alpha plus one over beta equals S over P. The condition matters, if either original root is zero, a reciprocal root does not exist.
Method.

To form a quadratic equation with new roots, call them u and v. First find their sum T equals u plus v and product U equals u v using S and P. Then write x squared minus T x plus U equals zero. Clear fractions by multiplying the whole equation by a nonzero common denominator. Any nonzero multiple describes the same equation, integer coefficients in their simplest ratio are usually preferred.

For squared roots, u equals alpha squared and v equals beta squared, so T equals S squared minus two P and U equals P squared. For cubed roots, T equals S cubed minus three P S and U equals P cubed. For reciprocal roots, T equals S over P and U equals one over P. A less direct transformation can still be handled systematically. If u equals alpha plus two over alpha and v equals beta plus two over beta, then T equals S plus two S over P and U equals P plus two open bracket alpha over beta plus beta over alpha close bracket plus four over P. Replace alpha over beta plus beta over alpha by open bracket S squared minus two P close bracket over P to finish entirely in S, P.
Official specification examples, inverse squares and cross reciprocals.

Let S equals alpha plus beta and P equals alpha beta is not equal to zero. For roots one over alpha squared, one over beta squared, combining fractions gives T equals open bracket alpha squared plus beta squared close bracket over open bracket alpha squared beta squared close bracket equals open bracket S squared minus two P close bracket over P squared and U equals one over open bracket alpha squared beta squared close bracket equals one over P squared. For roots alpha plus two over beta, beta plus two over alpha, the sum is T equals S plus two open bracket one over alpha plus one over beta close bracket equals S plus two S over P. Expanding the product gives U equals alpha beta plus two plus two plus four over open bracket alpha beta close bracket equals P plus four plus four over P. Here the cross terms are each two, keep the denominator attached to the correct root. In either case form x squared minus T x plus U equals zero and clear denominators throughout. These transformations appear in Pearson's official F P one specification, section two point three, printed p.33. Worked example.

The roots of x squared minus five x plus six equals zero are alpha, beta. Form the quadratic with roots alpha squared, beta squared. S equals five and P equals six from the coefficients. The new sum is T equals S squared minus two P equals twenty five minus twelve equals thirteen, the new product is U equals P squared equals thirty six. Therefore the required equation is x squared minus thirteen x plus thirty six equals zero. Check, the old roots are two, three, whose squares are four, nine, their sum is thirteen and product thirty six.
Traps.

Trap, Taking the root sum as b over a. Why it's wrong, The x coefficient of a open bracket x minus alpha close bracket open bracket x minus beta close bracket is minus a open bracket alpha plus beta close bracket. Instead, Use minus b over a.
Trap, Writing alpha squared plus beta squared equals S squared. Why it's wrong, S squared contains two alpha beta. Instead, Subtract two P.
Trap, Applying a root transformation to the coefficients individually. Why it's wrong, Coefficients encode a sum and product, and these change together. Instead, Find the transformed T, U first.
Exam technique.

For Find or Calculate, state S and P, show the identity used and simplify to an exact fraction or integer. For Show that or Prove, show the expansion or algebraic identity and every substitution leading to the given result. For Hence, use the relation established in the earlier part. A quick check by solving the original quadratic can detect arithmetic slips, but the sum and product method is usually shorter and still works when explicit roots are awkward.
